subject: Anthropology
title: Subsistence Strategies
description: A micro-lesson that makes Subsistence Strategies usable.

hook.text: Some people hunt. Some farm. Some herd. How you get food shapes everything else about your society.

buildup.text: Anthropologists classify subsistence into foraging, pastoralism, horticulture, agriculture, and industrialism.

discovery.text: Foragers are often egalitarian. Farmers develop hierarchy. Your food system shapes your political system.

twist.text: The agricultural revolution wasn't progress for everyone. Early farmers were shorter, sicker, and worked harder.

climax.text: Subsistence isn't just about eating. It determines social structure, gender roles, settlement, and power.

punchline.text: Tell me how you eat and I'll tell you how you live.

quiz.question: How does subsistence strategy affect society?
options: It shapes social structure, gender roles, and power
It has no effect on politics

details.summary: Subsistence strategies are the methods societies use to obtain food — foraging, horticulture, pastoralism, agriculture, and industrialism. Each strategy shapes social organization, population density, settlement patterns, and cultural values in predictable ways.
details.whyItMatters: How people get food determines nearly everything about social organization. Subsistence strategies explain why some societies are egalitarian while others are stratified, why some are mobile while others build cities.
takeaways: Major strategies include foraging, horticulture, pastoralism, agriculture
Subsistence shapes social organization and settlement patterns
Food procurement methods determine much about cultural systems

faq.question: What is the difference between horticulture and agriculture?
faq.answer: Horticulture uses simple tools and shifting cultivation without plowing or irrigation. Agriculture involves intensive techniques — plowing, irrigation, fertilization — that produce larger surpluses but require more labor and support larger populations.

faq.question: Why did most societies eventually adopt agriculture?
faq.answer: Agriculture supports larger populations per unit area. Once neighboring groups adopted it and grew, non-agricultural societies faced competitive pressure. However, the transition was neither universal nor always beneficial for individual health and wellbeing.
